articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities for Counter Narcotics and Cyber-related Activities, Issues New General License
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting entities involved in counter narcotics and cyber-related activities. This action aims to disrupt illicit networks that pose threats to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued a new Illicit Drugs General License to facilitate certain transactions and an amended Russia-related General License. The agency also published updated Frequently Asked Questions to provide further guidance on the scope and implications of these new measures.
These actions underscore OFAC's ongoing commitment to combating illicit activities through the strategic use of financial sanctions and the provision of clear guidance to ensure compliance.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) of the U.S. Department of the Treasury today announced new counter terrorism designations. These designations target individuals and entities identified as supporting terrorist organizations and activities globally.

The action is part of a broader effort to disrupt the financial networks of terrorist groups, limiting their ability to fund operations and procure resources. These measures aim to protect the U.S. financial system from abuse by those who seek to finance terrorism.
Further details regarding the specific individuals and entities designated, as well as the implications for financial institutions, are available on the Treasury Department's website.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Joint Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced a series of designations targeting individuals and entities involved in both counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. This coordinated action highlights the nexus between these illicit enterprises.

These designations aim to sever the financial lifelines of criminal organizations that engage in drug trafficking and simultaneously provide support to terrorist groups. By targeting these intertwined networks, OFAC seeks to enhance global security and stability.
Financial institutions are advised to review their compliance programs to ensure they are adequately screening for these newly designated parties and mitigating associated risks.

articles.headline: OFAC Updates Iran Designation Information
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an update regarding existing Iran designations. This update provides additional information and clarifications concerning previously sanctioned individuals and entities linked to Iran.

These updates are part of OFAC's ongoing efforts to maintain the effectiveness and integrity of its sanctions programs. The agency regularly reviews and refines its listings to ensure accuracy and to address evolving threats.
Financial institutions and other regulated entities should consult the updated information to ensure their compliance measures reflect the latest details on Iran-related sanctions.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-related Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting individuals and entities connected to Iran. These actions are part of the ongoing pressure campaign against the Iranian regime.

The designations aim to disrupt networks supporting Iran's destabilizing activities, including its proliferation of weapons and support for regional proxy groups. These measures seek to limit the regime's access to the international financial system.
All U.S. persons and entities are generally prohibited from engaging in transactions with those designated, and any assets under U.S. jurisdiction belonging to these parties are blocked.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities for Cyber-related and Transnational Criminal Activities, Issues Cuba Sanctions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting entities involved in cyber-related activities and transnational criminal organizations. Concurrently, OFAC has issued new Cuba designations and published a Cuba-related determination.

These actions are aimed at disrupting malicious cyber actors and criminal networks that pose threats to U.S. national security and economic stability. The Cuba designations further reinforce existing sanctions against the Cuban regime.
The publication of the Cuba-related determination provides additional clarity on specific aspects of the Cuba sanctions program, guiding compliance for affected parties.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-related Designations, Amends Venezuela General License
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations and provided updates to certain existing Iran-related listings. These actions are part of the ongoing strategy to counter Iran's illicit activities.

In addition to the Iran-focused measures, OFAC issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a corresponding Frequently Asked Question. This amendment aims to provide clarity and potentially adjust the scope of authorized activities under the Venezuela sanctions program.
An Iran-related OFAC Alert was also published, advising stakeholders on potential risks and compliance considerations associated with transactions involving Iran.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an amended Iran-related General License. This amendment modifies existing authorizations for certain transactions involving Iran.

General Licenses are issued to permit specific types of transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under sanctions programs. This particular amendment aims to refine the scope of permissible activities, potentially easing or clarifying restrictions in certain areas.
Parties engaging in Iran-related transactions are advised to review the amended General License carefully to ensure ongoing compliance with U.S. sanctions regulations.

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Sanctions on North Korea and Democratic Republic of the Congo
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting entities and individuals associated with North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). These actions aim to counter illicit activities in both regions.

The North Korea designations are part of ongoing efforts to curb the regime's weapons of mass destruction programs and its illicit revenue generation. The DRC-related designations address human rights abuses and corruption within the country.
These sanctions underscore the U.S. commitment to promoting human rights, stability, and non-proliferation globally by targeting those who undermine these principles.

articles.headline: OFAC Reaches Settlement Agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc.
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc. This settlement resolves apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations.

Settlement agreements typically involve a company agreeing to pay a civil monetary penalty and implement enhanced compliance measures to prevent future violations. These actions serve as a reminder of the importance of robust sanctions compliance programs.
Details of the settlement, including the specific violations and the agreed-upon penalty, are available on the OFAC website.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Pays $1,529,685 to Settle OFAC Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc. has agreed to pay a civil monetary penalty of $1,529,685 to the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to settle apparent violations of sanctions regulations. This settlement underscores the importance of robust compliance programs for companies operating internationally.

The enforcement action highlights OFAC's continued focus on ensuring that U.S. companies adhere strictly to sanctions requirements, particularly concerning transactions with sanctioned jurisdictions or entities.
Companies are reminded to conduct thorough due diligence and implement effective internal controls to prevent unauthorized transactions that could lead to significant penalties.

articles.headline: Bank of America, N.A. Fined $11,662,930 by OFAC for Sanctions Breaches
body: Bank of America, N.A. has been assessed a civil monetary penalty of $11,662,930 by the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for apparent violations of sanctions regulations. This penalty is part of a coordinated enforcement action that also involved FinCEN and the OCC.

The violations stemmed from the bank's failure to report suspicious activity and processing payments that apparently violated sanctions. OFAC's enforcement release identified 475 apparent violations, totaling approximately $14.8 million, from September 2021 to April 2025.

These violations included 403 payments, amounting to $14.3 million, sent to or through 35 blocked banks, and issues with alert prioritization and watchlist updates that allowed designated individuals and other blocked parties to transact. The breaches spanned various sanctions programs, including those related to Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and terrorism.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Pays $175,015 for OFAC Sanctions Violations
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics has paid a civil monetary penalty of $175,015 to the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for apparent violations of sanctions regulations. This action highlights the responsibility of logistics companies in ensuring compliance with U.S. sanctions.

The penalty serves as a reminder that all entities involved in international trade and logistics must implement robust compliance programs to prevent facilitating transactions that violate OFAC regulations.
OFAC continues to enforce sanctions vigorously across various industries to safeguard U.S. national security and foreign policy objectives.

articles.headline: Individual Fined $1,427,230 by OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: An individual has been assessed a civil monetary penalty of $1,427,230 by the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for apparent violations of sanctions regulations. This enforcement action underscores that individuals, as well as corporations, are subject to OFAC's jurisdiction and penalties.
OFAC's actions against individuals demonstrate the agency's commitment to holding all parties accountable for breaches of sanctions law, regardless of their organizational affiliation.
This penalty serves as a deterrent and a reminder of the severe consequences for engaging in transactions prohibited by U.S. sanctions programs.

articles.headline: IMF Head Warns AI Demand Will Drive Global Interest Rate Hikes
body: Kristalina Georgieva, Managing Director of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), has issued a warning that the surging global demand for artificial intelligence (AI) will compel central banks worldwide to increase interest rates. This demand for AI hardware and related technology products is contributing to rising consumer prices globally.

Georgieva, speaking at the 2026 Apec summit in Shenzhen, indicated that these AI-driven inflationary pressures, coupled with the ongoing energy shock from the Middle East conflict, are expected to push global inflation to 4.7% this year. Central banks, including the European Central Bank, the U.S. Federal Reserve, and the Bank of England, have already raised rates this year in response to inflationary pressures.

Despite these headwinds, the rapid deployment of AI is also contributing to stronger-than-expected economic growth in several countries. Financial markets anticipate further increases in borrowing costs next year as AI continues to bolster economic activity amidst a volatile global landscape.

articles.headline: European Commission's Autumn Forecast: Continued Growth Amidst Higher Inflation
body: The European Commission's Autumn 2026 Economic Forecast indicates that the EU economy performed better than expected in the first three quarters of 2026 and is set to continue expanding. This resilience comes despite heightened global uncertainties, challenging energy market conditions, and persistent inflationary pressures.

Inflation in the euro area reached 4% in October and is projected to peak above 4% between late 2026 and early 2027 before gradually easing. While energy inflation is expected to moderate next year, food inflation is set to accelerate due to higher energy and fertilizer costs and crop disruptions from extreme summer weather.

Job growth is anticipated to slow, but the unemployment rate is expected to remain near its record low of 6%. Wages are projected to slightly outpace inflation, leading to moderate positive real wage growth.

Kuwait and Bahrain reported intercepting Iranian aerial attacks on Wednesday. These events highlight the escalating tensions in the Middle East, with concerns about threats to energy infrastructure and maritime trade remaining high.

The ongoing conflict in the Middle East continues to expose businesses and consumers to significant energy-price uncertainty, with physical shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on energy infrastructure being key watchpoints.

articles.headline: China, Japan, South Korea Address Geopolitical Disruptions at ASEAN Summit
body: China, Japan, and South Korea convened at the 29th ASEAN Plus Three Summit in Manila to discuss growing geopolitical disruptions and their impact on regional stability. Leaders called for stronger cooperation to address shared challenges, including rising food and energy prices affecting East and Southeast Asia.

Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., chair of ASEAN, emphasized that disruptions thousands of miles away are having immediate impacts on people across the region. He urged for tangible benefits of regional cooperation to reach citizens with urgency, providing greater security and confidence.

Chinese Agriculture Minister Zhang Zhu warned of rising geopolitical tensions, slowing global economic growth, and overlapping risks, while acknowledging East Asia's remarkable economic achievements. The region continues to face challenges related to energy supplies, food security, and supply chain stability.

Among the actions, American Express National Bank in Sandy, Utah, received a Cease and Desist Order and a $350 million civil money penalty for BSA compliance program deficiencies, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and customer due diligence and identification program violations.

articles.headline: BIS Implements New Export Controls on Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors and Rescinds AI Diffusion Rule
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has issued an interim final rule, effective November 19, 2026, significantly amending the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to address concerns about foreign entities circumventing U.S. export controls by remotely accessing advanced computing technology. This rule formally rescinds the previous AI Diffusion Rule, replacing it with more targeted restrictions.

The new regulations impose a destination-based license requirement for exports, reexports, or in-country transfers of advanced computing items to five additional countries: Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand. A new end-use-based license requirement also applies to advanced computing items destined for non-U.S. data centers that provide remote access to a significant volume of compute power to end users headquartered in Macau or Country Group D:5 destinations, which include China, Belarus, and Russia.

The rule also tightens presumptions for front-end fabricators and outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) companies when exporting advanced-node logic chips, particularly when the integrated circuit designer is located in or has an ultimate parent company headquartered in Country Group D:1, D:4, or D:5 destinations, or Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil. Comments on these revisions are due by January 19, 2027.
articles.source: U.S. Department of Commerce BIS / Federal Register

articles.headline: BIS Extends Suspension of End-User Controls for Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has announced an extension of the suspension of the interim final rule titled "Expansion of End-User Controls to Cover Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities." The suspension, which was set to expire on November 9, 2026, will now continue through January 10, 2027.

This extension impacts amendments to 15 CFR parts 732, 734, 736, 744, and 748 that were initially published in September 2025 and subsequently stayed. The "Affiliates Rule" aimed to expand end-user controls to include affiliates of certain listed entities.
The decision to further suspend the rule provides additional time for stakeholders to adjust and for BIS to potentially refine its approach to these complex export control measures.
articles.source: Federal Register / Bureau of Industry and Security

articles.headline: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors
body: In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)--countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. The regulatory changes in this rule formalize the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced in May 2025.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
